passage: After the Sunday class at the community centre, Aparna stayed on the lobby bench with a blank card from the notice-board tray. Six years since she and her brother Akash last spoke. She wrote three openings and crossed out all of them. The instructor passed with a bunch of keys and asked whether she needed anything; Aparna said, "Just a difficult note." What she finally wrote was: "Akash, it has been too long. I said cruel things about your wedding and never took them back. I am sorry. You do not have to reply. I would like to hear how you are, whenever you want." She did not add a list of who had hurt whom. At the post box outside, her hand paused. Then the card went in.

qa.q: How many years since Aparna and Akash last spoke?
What might Aparna's paused hand at the post box show?
qa.a: Nervousness about reaching out and fear of how Akash will respond, before she decides to go ahead.

qa.q: What in the note leaves Akash room to decide?
qa.a: It says Akash does not have to reply and asks for news only whenever Akash wants.

qa.q: How might Akash feel on receiving the card?
qa.a: He may feel surprised, wary or moved, and the lack of demands lets him respond at his own pace.

grounding: The protagonist reaches out to a sibling after years of silence with a short humble note that owns her part and demands no accounting.

passage:
I'm Alka, and my brother Lalit and I didn't speak for four years. It started with an argument about our mother's hospital bills and ended with both of us saying things we couldn't take back.

For years I waited for him to call first. He didn't. Neither did I.

Last month I saw a photo of his son's first birthday on a cousin's feed. A nephew I'd never held. Something in my chest cracked.

I wrote maybe fifteen drafts. The long ones explained everything, who said what, who was wrong. I deleted them all. The one I sent was four lines: "Lalit, I miss you. I'm sorry for what I said about Papa's money. I'd like to meet your son someday. No pressure."

He replied the next evening: "Me too. Sunday?"

We had chai. It was awkward. We didn't go over the whole fight. Since then, I've sent him a message every week. Small things. That's how it's coming back.

qa.q: How many years did Alka and Lalit not speak?
qa.a: They didn't speak for four years.

qa.q: What did Alka feel on seeing the photo of Lalit's son's birthday?
qa.a: Alka felt a crack of grief and longing for a brother and a nephew missed for so long.

qa.q: Why did Alka's short message work better than the long drafts?
qa.a: It was humble, owned Alka's part and asked for nothing big, avoiding a full accounting of the fight, so Lalit could say yes easily.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt when he read Alka's message?
qa.a: Lalit likely felt relieved and moved, replying quickly that he missed Alka too.

grounding: A spoken account shows someone reaching out to a sibling after years of silence with a short, humble note, owning their part without demanding a full accounting, and rebuilding trust with small acts.

passage:
First Sunday of March. Omkar sat on his balcony in Nagpur with his phone. Three years since he and Ojas had stopped talking, after Omkar skipped Ojas's engagement over a work trip and then said something cruel when Ojas complained. He missed his little brother so much it felt like a stone in his stomach. He typed: "Ojas, I'm sorry I missed your engagement, and for what I said after. I was wrong. I miss you." He sent it before he could delete it.

Thursday. Ojas replied: "Thanks for saying it." Nothing more. Omkar felt a pang, but didn't push. He didn't ask Ojas to explain his side.

Three weeks later. Omkar had sent a message every few days: a photo of their old school, a cricket score, a birthday wish for Ojas's wife. On Saturday Ojas wrote: "Coming to Nagpur next month. Lunch?" Omkar read it standing up, grinning.

qa.q: What did Omkar skip that started the silence?
qa.a: He skipped Ojas's engagement over a work trip.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling on the balcony that first Sunday?
qa.a: Omkar felt a heavy longing and regret, missing his brother like a stone in his stomach.

qa.q: How did Omkar rebuild trust after Ojas's short reply?
qa.a: He didn't push or demand Ojas's side, and kept sending small, steady messages until Ojas suggested lunch.

qa.q: How might Ojas have felt reading Omkar's first message?
qa.a: Ojas may have felt cautious but touched, acknowledging the apology while still guarded.

grounding: The story shows a young man who reaches out to his brother after years of silence with a short, humble apology, owns his part without demanding an accounting, and rebuilds trust with small, steady acts.
